(d) by when Government are likely to take a decision;

workers, in due course; 
(f) if so, the details thereof;

8 

[15 May, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) At the time of 
formulation of Vth Five year Plan the need for delivery of a package of 
service in an integrated manner was realized for development of children and the 
Intergrated Child Development Service (ICDS) Scheme was launched in 
1975 in 33 ICDS projects with the following objectives:— 
(i) to improve the nutritional and health status of children below the age of 
six years and pregnant and lactating mothers; 
(ii) to lay the foundation for the proper psychological, physical and 
social development of the child; 
(iii) to reduce the incidence of mortality, morbidity, malnutrition and 
school drop-outs; 
(iv) to achieve effective coordination of policy and implementation 
among various departments to promote child development; 
(v) to enhance the capability of the mother to look after the normal health 
and nutritional needs of the child through proper health and nutrition 
education. 
The scheme provides a package of services comprising supplementary 
nutrition, immunization, referral services, health check-up, pre-school non-
formal and nutrition & health education. Anganwadi is the focal point of 
delivery of services under the Scheme. 
The Scheme was gradually expanded to 5626 Projects till the end of Ninth 
Plan. In Tenth Plan no expansion was allowed. However, in view of present 
Government's commitment, as enunciated in the National Common Minimum 
Programme, the Scheme has been expanded to 466 additional projects and 1.88 
lakh AWCs in 2005-06. 
(b) In Rajasthan, 4136 AWCs in 28 tribal projectsand 31676 AWCs in 229 
non-tribal projects have been set up. 
(c) and (d) Government of Rajasthan has sent a proposal for sanction of 4 Urban 
Projects, 1510Anganwadi Centres and 2681 Mini-AWCs, which is under 
consideration. 
(e) No, Sir. 
(f) Does not arise. 
(g) and (h) The performance of the ICDS Scheme has been evaluated by 
several agencies in the past, the latest being the one conducted by 
9 

RAJYA SABHA [15 May, 2006] 
National Institute of Public Cooperation and Child Development (NIPCCD) in 
2005-06. The preliminary findings of the appraisal conducted by NIPCCD, are as 
under:— 
• The percentage of severely malnourished children in the age gr oup 
0-3 years reduced from 7% in 1992 to 1% in 2006 and in case of 
children in the age group 3—5 years it reduced from 4% in 1992 
to 0.8% in 2006. 
• The percentage of children with low birth weight decreased from 
41 in 1992 to 29 in 2006. 
• The number of children in the age group 6 months-3 years 
registered for supplementary nutrition has increased from 45% to 57% 
between 1992—2006 of which 78% of the children are actually 
availing of supplementary nutrition; 
• In the case of children in the age group of 3—6 years, number of 
children registered increased from 56% to 63.5% out of which 75% 
are actually availing of supplementry nutrition. As regards pregnant 
and lactating mothers, the in crease in the number of those 
registered and availing of such facilities increased from 78% to 87% 
and from 78% to 89% respectively between 1992—2006. 
(i) and (I) UNICEF has been extending support for ICDS in terms of 
supplies of equipments such as weighing scales, photocopying machines, 
typewriters, growth charts, IFA tablets and technical support. As per Master Plan 
of Operation (2003—2007) UNISEFs financial support is of the order of US $ 56 
Million. Also United Nations under World Food Programme (WFP) has been 
providing supplementary nutrition in some ICDS Projects. At present, this 
support is being extended in 11 districts of 4 States viz., Madhya Pradesh, Orissa, 
Rajasthan and Uttaranchal with a budgetary support of US $ 7.20 Million for 
2004—2007.

*432. SHRI C. PERUMAL: Will the Mi nister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is proposed to bring electricity to all throughout the country by 
2007; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether any action plan has been formulated for the purpose; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a) and (b) 
With a view to expedite rural electrification programme in the .entry, 
Government of India has introduced "Rajiv Gandhi Grameen VidyutiKaran 
Yojana" (RGGVY) in April, 2005. The scheme covers electrification of all the 
villages in the country except the villages under the programme of Ministry of 
Non-conventional Energy Sources (MNES) for providing electricity from non-
conventional energy sources under their remove village electrification 
programme. 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
25 

RAJYA SABHA [15 May, 2006] 
The salient features of the RGGVY are as under:— 
1. Scheme is for the attainment of National Common Minimum 
Programme (NCMP) goal of providing access to electricity to all rural 
households and electrification of all villages over a period of four years. 
2. Creation of Rural Electricity Distribution Backbone (REDB) with one 
33/11 kV (or 66/11 kV) substation in every block appropriately linked to 
the State Transmission System. 
3. Creation of Village Electricity Infrastructure (VEI) for electrification of 
all un-electrified villages/habitations and provision of distribution 
transformer(s) of appropriate capacity in every village/habitation. 
4. Decentralized Distributed Generation (DDG) and Supply System from 
conventional sources for Villages/Habitations where grid supply is not cost 
effective and where Ministry of Non-Conventional Energy Sources would 
not be providing electricity through their programme(s). 
5. REDB, VEI and DDG would also cater to the requirement of 
agriculture and other activities which would facilitate overall rural 
development, employment generation and poverty alleviation. 
6. The scheme inter alia provides for financing of electrificaiton of all 
un-electrified Below Poverty Line (BPL) households in the country 
with 100% capital subsidy as per norms of Kutir Jyoti Programme in 
all rural habitations. 
7. Under this scheme 90% Capital Subsidy would be provided for 
projects. 
8. In the management of rural distribution through franchisees who could 
be Non-Governmental Organizations (NGOs), Users Association, 
Cooperatives or Individual entrep reneurs, the Panchayat institutions 
would be associated. The franchisees arrangement could be for system 
beyond and including feeders from substation or from and including 
Distribution Transformers(s). 
9. For projects to be eligible for capital subsidy under the scheme, prior 
commitment of the States  would also be obtained before sanction of 
projects under the scheme for:— 
• deployment of franchisees for the management of rural distribution 
in projects financed under the scheme, and

• the provision of requisite revenue subsidies to the State Utilities as 
required under the Electricity Act, 2003. 
10. Services of CPSUs have been offered to the states for assisting them in 
the execution of rural electrification projects as per their willingness 
and requirement.

like Korea, where it is around 2.47 per cent and their corproate sector share is 
only 3-4 per cent; and

least 2 per cent of the GDP and R and D is critical for improving 
productivity?

SIBAL): (a) and (b) No, Sir. as per the latest available official statistics, 2004-
05 the R&D expenditure as percentage of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) during 
the year 2002-03 was around 0.80% of which 25% was contributed by 
corporate sector comprising public and private industries. Incase of developed 
countries, the R&D expenditure is of the order of 2 to 3% of GDP of which major 
contribution comes from the corporate sector. For example, in Korea, indstry 
contributes about 75% of the total R&D expenditure. However, any 
comprison of these numbers and any

[15 May, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
conclusions drawn will be unrealistic inview of the resources and 
infrastructure available in the country. 
(c) The "Science and Technology Policy 2003" announced by the 
Government envisages to raise the level of investment on Science and 
Technology to at least 2% of GDP by the end of Tenth Plan with enhanced 
participation of R&D investment by industry. Accordingly, the Government has 
enhanced the S&T Plan outlay of Scientific Department from Rs. 12,022 
crores in Ninth Plan to Rs. 25,243 crores in Tenth Plan. Also, several initiatives 
have been taken to encourage investment on R&D both in industry and 
institutions through several fiscal incentives and other support measures such 
as support in the form of grants for industrial R&D projects, support to R&D

Food processing industry in Himachal Pradesh 
*435. SHRIMATI VIPLOVE THAKUR:  Will the Minister of FOOD 
PROCESSING INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Himachal's economy and the livelihood of a vast majority of its 
people depends on its fruit production, yet Himachal Pradesh loses out because 
no or little investment has gone into creating a food processing industry; and 
(b) whether any steps are being take n to augment and build special 
packages for Himachal Pradesh with regard to the food processing industry? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF FOOD 
PROCESSING INDUSTRIES (SHRI SUBODH KANT SAHAY): (a) and (b) 
Himachal Pradesh is rich in produc tion of horticulture produce including 
fruits. Government has implemented several plan schemes for promotion of 
food processing industries in Himachal Pradesh. Under these schemes, financial 
assistance is provided for technology upgradation/ modernization/establishment of 
the food processing units. Assistance is also provided for creation of 
infrastructure, support for R&D and human resource development besides other 
promotional measures to encourage development of the food processing 
industries. Enhanced quantum of assistance is available under the plan schemes 
for difficult areas including 
29 

RAJYA SABHA [15 May, 2006] 
Himachal Pradesh. Fruit processing capacity in Himachal Pradesh is 
estimated at 80,500 MT per annum. 
Recognizing the potential of horticulture for socio economic development of the 
hilly states including Himachal Pradesh, the Govt, of India has extended the 
Technology Mission for Integrated Development of Horticulture in North Eastern 
States (including Sikkim) to Himachal Pradesh along with Jammu & Kashmir 
and Uttaranchal. The goals of the Mission are to establish convergence and 
synergy among various on-going Governmental Programmes in the field of 
horticulture development to achieve horizontal and vertical integration of these 
Programmes. Technology Mission consists of four Mini Missions to address various 
aspects of horticulture development including research, production, post harvest 
management, marketing and processing. Mini Mission-IV is concerned with 
processing which is implemented through Ministry of Food Processing 
Industries. 
The Fruit & vegetable processing units are already exempted from 
payment of excise duty. In the year 2004-05 the Government has allowed under 
Income Tax Act, a deduction of 100% of profit for five years and 25% of profits for 
the next five years in case of new agro processing industries set up to process, 
preserve and package fruits and vegetables. In the Union Budget of 2006-07, 
Government has announced exemption of excise duty on condensed milk, 
icecream, preparation of meat, fish and poultry, pectins, pasta and yeast. Custom 
duty on packaging machines has been reduced from 15 percent to 5 percent. 
NABARD has created a separate window with a corpus of 1,000 crore for 
refinancing loans to the sector, especially for agro-processing infrastructure and 
market development. The incentives available for the food processing sector and 
special measures taken under the Horticulture Technology Mission are likely 
to create a conducive environment in Himachal Pradesh for attracting more 
investment in Food Processing Industry.

 3022. SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR: 
Will the Minister of FOOD PROCESSING INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the food industry is expected to grow at 8-8.5 per cent as per a 
study conducted by the industry; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the details of the policy packages announced by Government to give a 
further boost to this industry; and 
(d) what is the position of Orissa in this sector and the action plan of the 
Centre to help the State to improve the prospects of this industry in the rural 
areas of the State? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF FOOD 
PROCESSING INDUSTRIES (SHRI SUBODH KANT SAHAY): (a) and (b) 
As per the report of M/s Rabo India Finance Private Limited, processed food 
industry in India should aim to grow at about 10% per annum between 2005—
2015. 
(c) In order to give boost to growth of FPI sector the Government has 
allowed under Income Tax Act, a deduction of 100% of profit for five years 
and 25% of profits for the next five years in case of new agro processing 
industries set up to process, preserve and package fruits and vegetables. 
Excise duty of 16% on dairy machinery has been fully waived for promotion 
of dairy processing industries. In the Budget of 2005-06 excise duty of Rs. 
1.00 per kg. on refined edible oil and Rs. 1.25 per kg. on vanaspati was 
abolished. Customs duty on refrigerated vans was reduced from 20% to 10%. 
In the Budget 2006-07 the Government has waived excise duty on condensed 
milk, ice cream, preparations of meat, fish and poultry, pectins, pasta and 
yeast. Excise duty on ready-to-eat packaged foods and instant food mixes, 
like dosa and idli mixes has been reduced from 16 per cent to 8 per cent. 
Excise duty on aerated drinks has been reduced from 24 per cent to 16 per 
cent. Food processing to be priority sector for bank credit; NABARD to 
create a refinancing window with a corpus of Rs. 1000 crore for agro 
processing infrastructure and market development. 
(d) The Government has already formul ated Plan Schemes for providing 
financial assistance to food processing sector which are project specific

Capacity of sea-food processing industry 
3023. CHRI T.T.V. DHINAKARAN: Will the Minister of FOOD 
PROCESSING INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that sea-food processing industry In the country is utilizing 
only around 20 per cent of its capacity; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) the steps taken by Government for reaching full-capacity utilization with specific 
reference to availability of new material; and 
(d) whether Government will consider to review its policy on sea-food industry to 
provide impetus to this industry? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF FOOD 
PROCESSING INDUSTRIES (SHRI SUBODH KANT SAHAY):(a) to (d) The see-food 
processing industry in the country is utilizing only about 20 per cent of the annual installed 
capacity primarily due to shortage of raw material and increase in domestic demand of fish 
which is growing at an annual rate of 2.4 per cent. However, the utilization goes up in 
peak seasons. 
Government have taken various measures to improve the availability of raw material 
for better capacity utilization and consequent growth of sea-food processing industry, 
which include inter alia the following:— 
(i) Development of deep sea fishing for harvesting under exploited resources such 
as tuna, cephalopods and Pelagie finfish. 
(ii) Increase of production by processing aquaculture of fresh water and blackish 
water through Fish Farmers Development Agencies which includes development 
of new farms, renovation of existing farms, farming inputs etc. 
(iii) Promotional activities and financial schemes for the farmers for sustainable 
shrimp/scampi culture in India. 
47 

RAJYA SABHA [15 May, 2006] 
(iv) Development of infrastructure for setting up of fishing harbours and 
fish landing centres. 
(v) Assistance for motorization of traditional crafts and conversion of 
trawlers into long liners. 
(vi) Promulgation of comprehensive marine fishing policy addressing 
conservation and management issues. 
(vii) Enactment of Coastal Aquaculture Authority Act for ensuring 
sustainable development of coastal aquaculture. 
(viii) Encouraging processors to import raw material for reprocessing and 
export.

The major various activities of the Ministiy taken up during the last five years are 
broadly divided into two major categories viz., Programmes of Societal benefit of 
coastal population and Programmes of national interests. These include (i) 
Development of Desalination Technology, (ii) Lobster technology, (iii) 
Potential Fishing zone advisories, (iv) Ocean State Forecast, (v) Early Tsunami 
Warning System, (vi) Marine Living Resources, (vii) Coastal Zone Management,

being of the nation in general and those living near the ocean, are as follows: 
Societal benefit of coastal po pulation are (i) Development and

Power policy 
3119. SHRI EKANATH K. THAKUR: W ill the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to follow a differential power policy 
approach for public and private sectors to achieve the ambitious goal of 
generating 60 GW power by the year 2012; and 
(b) if so, the details of the proposed differential policy? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) and (b) 
To achieve the goal of providing power to all by 2012, a capacity of more than 
1,00,000 MW is required to be added in Tenth and Eleventh Plans. National 
Electricity Policy provides that power being most crucial infrastructure, public 
sector investments, both at the Central and State Governments, will have to be 
stepped up. Considering the magnitude of the expansion of the sector required, 
a sizeable part of the investments will also need to be brought in from the private 
sector. The Electricity Act, 2003 creates a conducive environment for investments 
in all segments of the industry, both by the public sector and private sector, by 
removing barrier to entry in different segments. Section 63 of the Act provides 
for participation of suppliers on competitive basis in different segments which 
will further encourage private sector investment. 
The Tariff Policy notified by Central Government under the provisions of the 
Electricity Act, 2003 stipulates that all future requirement of power should be 
procured competitively by distribution licensees except in cases of expansion of 
existing projects or where there is a State controlled/ owned company as an 
identified developer, where regulators will need to resort to tariff determination 
based on norms. The policy further stipulates that even for the Public Sector 
projects, tariff of all new generation and transmission projects should be decided 
on the basis of competitive bidding after a period of five years. 
Shortage of gas in power plants 
3120. SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether both private and public sector gas-based power plants are facing 
acute shortage of gas, curtailing the Plant Load Factor to 60 per cent; 
(b) whether there have been no substantial increases in gas production by 
ONGC facilities and delays in development of gas blocks by private operators 
like Reliance and GSPCL; and 
127 

RAJYA SABHA [15 May, 2006] 
(c) whether this gas crunch is also affecting the financial closure of a 
number of gas-based power projects? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) Yes, 
Sir. The private as well as public sector gas based power plants are facing acute 
shortage of gas. During the year 2005-2006 against the normative requirement of 
gas (for operation of gas power plants at 90% PLF) of 52.66 Million Metric 
Standard Cubic Meter per day (MMSCMD), the average supply was only 35.37 
MMSCMD which was adequate for operation of the plants at about 60% PLF. 
(b) There has been a marginal declin e in gas production of ONGC over 
the last few years due to ageing of fields, majority of which have entered 
the natural decline phase. 
NTPC Ltd., in the process to tie-up fuel for its Kawas and Gandhar 
Combined Cycle Power Project Stage-II, had issued Letter of Intent on M/s 
Reliance Industries Ltd., which was accepted by them. Subsequently, after series 
of discussion M/s RIL offered commencement of gas supplies in the time window 
between December, 2007 to December, 2008. NTPC Ltd., however, requested 
M/s RIL to expedite commencement of gas supplies from the end of 
2006/early 2007. 
(c) Many proposals for gas based power plants which were planned 
for commissioning during the last year of Tenth Plan and in the beginning 
of Eleventh Plan have been delayed due to non-tie up of gas availability. 
These projects could, therefore, not achieve financial closure.

Tehri Dam Project 
3127. SHRIMATI HEMA MALINI: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the mega 2400 MW Tehri Dam Project has been 
hanging fire for several years due to non-rehabilitation of displaced persons and 
other issues; and 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the Northern State of Uttaranchal has 
displaced an estimated 100,000 persons and plunging 125 villages under a vast 
artificial lake? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) The 
2400 MW Tehri Hydro Power Complex comprises of Tehri Dam & Hydro 
Power Plant (HPP) Stage-I (1000MW), Koteshwar Dam & HPP (400 MW) and 
Tehri Pumped Storage Plant (PSP) (1000MW). Government of India 
140 

[15 May, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
had approved the execution of Tehri Stage-I (1000 MW) in March, 1994 along 
with committed and essential works of Koteshwar Project and Pumped 
Storage Plant. The implementation of Tehri Stage-I had been affected due to 
various problems viz. 
(i) Agitation confronting the project in the initial period and after 
accord of Government approval, which delayed the raising of the crucial 
Coffer Dam to a safe height. 
(ii) Due to local agitation including agitation by the VHP, closure of 
Diversion Tunnels T-3 and T-4 scheduled for November/December, 1999 
was delayed and the tunnels could be closed only in January, 2001. 
(iii) Due to poor rock strata, there was sudden rockfall in Shaft T-3 of Right 
Bank Spilway in August, 2004 delaying closure of the last Diversion 
Tunnel T-2. 
(iv) PILs filed in the High Court of Uttaranchal restraining closure of 
Diversion Tunnel T-2. Diversion Tunnel T-2 could be closed on 
29.10.2005 with the permission of the High Court. 
(v) Constitution of various Committees to examine the issues relating to 
Rehabilitation and Resettlement , Environment, Safety, Self-
Purification quality of Gangajal, etc. 
According to Government of Uttara nchal, who are looking after the 
Rehabilitation & Resettlement Works, Tehri Hydo Project (2400 MW) is not 
delayed due to non-rehabilitation of displaced persons because land and other 
benefits as per Rehabilitation Policy, 1988 have already been given to all effected 
urban and rural families upto RL 790 M in submergence area. 
The 260.5 high Earth and Rockfull Dam has been raised to its full height. Two 
units of 250 MW each of Tehri HEP Stage-I (1000MW) have been rolled on 
31.03.2006 and commissioning of the units is expected shortly. 
Government of India approved implementation of Koteshwar Project (400 MW) 
in April, 2000 and the works on this project are in full swing. The Tehri Pumped 
Storage Plant (1000 MW) has been cleared by the Public Investment Board 
and is awaiting investment approval of the Government.

Rajiv Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran Yojana 
3131. SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) what are the details of Rajiv Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran Yojana, along 
with the budgetary allocation; 
(b) the number of rural areas electrified so far under the scheme, State-wise 
along with the assistance released; 
(c) whether Karnataka Government has requested for assistance for 
implementation of the scheme in 9 more districts; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) The 
Government of India introduced "Rajiv Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran 
Yojana" (RGGVY) in April, 2005 for th e attainment of National Common 
Minimum Goal of providing access to electricity to all rural households over a 
period of four years. 
The salient features of the RGGVY are as under:— 
1. Scheme is for the attainment of National Common Minimum 
Programme (NCMP) goal of providing access to electricity to all rural 
households and electrification of all villages over a period of four 
years. 
2. Creation of Rural ELectricity Distribution Backbone (REDB) with one 
33/11 kV (or 66.11 kV) sub-station in every block appropriately linked to 
the State Transmission System. 
3. Creation of Village Electricity Infrastructure (VEI) for electrification of 
all unelectrified villages/ habitations and provision of distribution 
transformer(s) of appropriate capacity in every village/habitation. 
4. Decentralized Distributed Generation (DDG) and Supply System from 
conventional sources for Villages/Habitations where grid supply is 
not cost effective and where Ministry of Non-Conventional Energy 
Sources would not be providing electricity through their 
programme(s). 
5. REDB, VEI and DDG would also cater to the requirement of 
agriculture and other activities which would facilitate overall rural 
development, employment generation and poverty alleviation. 
151 

RAJYA SABHA [15 May, 2006] 
6. The scheme interalia provides for financing of eletrification of all un-
electrified Below Poverty Line (BPL) households in the country with 
100% capital subsidy as per norms of Kutir Jyoti Programme in all rural 
habitations. 
7. Under this scheme 90% Capital Subsidy would be provided for 
projects. 
8. In the management of rural distribution through franchisees who 
could be Non-Governmental Organizations (NGOs), Users 
Association, Cooperatives or individual entrepreneurs, the 
Panchayat institutions would be associated. The franchisees 
arrangement could be for system beyond and including feeders from 
substation or from and including Distribution Transformers). 
9. For projects to be eligible for capital subsidy under the scheme, prior 
commitment of the States would also be obtained before sanction of 
projects under the scheme for:— 
 
• deployment of franchisees for the management of rural 
distribution in projects financed under the scheme, and 
• the provision of requisite revenue subsidies to the State utilities as 
required under the Electricity Act, 2003. 
10. Services of CPSUs have been offered to the states for assisting them in 
the execution of rural electrification projects as per their willingness 
and requirement. 
For the year 2005-06, Rs. 1100 crore was allocated and for the current year 
Rs. 3000 crore have been allocated. 
(b) As per Report of Rural Electrification Corporation (REC), Village 
Electrification Infrastructure has been created in 9819 villages during 2005-
06 and a cumulative amount of Rs. 1512.06 crore so far has been disbursed 
under the Programme. State-wise deta ils are given in the Statement. (See 
below) 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. Karnataka Govenrment had sent 26 proposals to REC 
out of which 17 were approved at the cost of Rs. 375.39 crore. 9 projects 
were not sanctioned as the sanctioned limit of Rs. 5000 crore approved by 
Cabinet had been reached.

National Tariff Policy 
3133 SHRIMATI N. P. DURGA: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have come out with the National 
Tariff Policy to accelerate power sector reforms; and 
(b) in what manner the new National Tariff Policy addresses the 
contentious issues of calculating cross subsidy surcharge for open access 
in distribution? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a) The 
Central Government has notified the tariff policy on 6th January, 2006 under 
the provision of the Electricity Act, 2003. 
(b) The Tariff Policy provides that a consumer who is. permitted open 
access will have to make payment to the generator, the transmission licensee 
whose transmission systems are used, distribution utility for the wheeling 
charges and, in addition, the cross subsidy surcharge. The computation of cross 
subsidy surcharge, therefore, needs to be done in a manner that while it 
compensates the distribution licensee, it does not 
160 

[15 May, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
constrain introduction of competition through open access. A consumer would 
avail of open access only if the payment of all the charges leads to a benefit to 
him. The policy further states that while the interest of distribution licensee needs to 
be protected, it would be essential that this provision of the Act, which requires 
the open access to be introduced in a time-bound manner, is used to bring about 
competition in the larger interest of consumers. 
The Tariff Policy lays down the methodology for computation of cross 
subsidy surcharge. 
Restructuring of APDRP 
3134 SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: Will the Minister of POWER 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether in a bid to give a further push to promote States to encourage 
reduction in Aggregate Transmission and Commercial (AT&C) losses, 
Government propose to restructur e the ongoing Accelerated Power 
Development and Reforms Programme (APDRP); 
(b) if so, whether Government have admitted that the 36 per cent of AT&C 
losses and losses of Rs. 24,000 crore incurred by State Electricity Boards are the 
matter of serious concern; 
(c) if so, whether some of the States  like Maharashtra, Gujarat, Andhra 
Pradesh have been benefited by APDRP; and 
(d) if so. by what time other States are likely to be benefited by this reform? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) With a 
view to examine the issues relating to Accelerated Power Development and 
Reforms Programme (APDRP) including the achievements, the shortcomings, 
problems of implementations and to make suggestions for improvement, it has 
been decided to constitute a Task Force for restructuring of APDRP with the 
following terms of reference: 
(i) To assess the current efforts under APDRP; 
(ii) Analyze the current reforms initiatives that are being pursued by the 
States with reference to the objectives of APDRP; 
(iii) To assess the need for modifications in the light of independent 
evaluations and other feed back; and 
(iv) Suggest measures to achieve the objectives of APDRP. 
161 

RAJYA SABHA [15 May, 2006] 
(b) to (d) The Aggregate Technical and Commercial (AT&C) losses during 
2004-05 were 33.82 per cent and overall commercial losses (without subsidy) were 
Rs. 22,129 crore during the said period, which indeed is a serious concern for the 
Government. The steps taken by the Government to reduce the transmission and 
distribution losses including theft are: 
(i) Metering of 11 kV feeders and consumer metering; 
(ii) Energy accounting and auditing; 
(iii) Strengthening the provisions , relating to theft of power in 
Electricity Act, 2003; 
(iv) Upgradation and strengthening of sub-transmission and distribution 
system through implementation of Accelerated Power Development and 
Reforms Programme (APDRP); 
(v) Incentivising for reduction of cash losses by State power utilities under 
APDRP; 
(vi) Introduction of High Voltage Distribution System (HVDS); and 
(vii) Introduction of IT applications.

as grant to such Utilities that reduce cash losses over the base year of 2000-01.

aggregating to Rs. 19180.46 crores under investment component of APDRP, out of

Formation of a New Department of Earth Sciences 
3146 SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will the Minister of OCEAN 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government propose to form a new Department of 
Earth Sciences by merging Indian Meteorological Department and 
Department of Oceanography; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) whether this will be an improvement over the existing system of 
different departments? 
THE MINISTER OF OCEAN DEVELOPMENT (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): 
(a) and (b) Yes Sir, Government (Cabinet) has approved the reorganization of the 
Ministry of Ocean Development as Ministry of Earth Sciences. The Earth System 
Organization (ESO) as an executive mechanism under the Ministry of Earth 
Sciences would have two major entities, namely (i) Ocean Science and 
Technology Department and (ii) India Meteorological Department. The Ocean 
Science and Technology Department would consist of the existing Centres and 
Attached Offices of the Ministry of Ocean Development. The India 
Meteorological Department (IMD) would consist of the existing IMD, a 
strengthened Seismological Institute and the corres ponding components (like 
Earthquake Risk Evaluation Centre and programme personnel) from the 
Department of Science and Technology (DST). The Indian Institute of Tropical 
Meteorology (IITM) and National Centre for Medium Range Weather 
Forecasting (NCMRWF) would report to ESO. 
(c) Yes Sir, formation of Ministry of Earth Sciences will enable a 
framework for understanding the complex interactions among the key 
elements of the earth system, namely  the ocean, atmosphere and the solid 
earth, by encompassing the functioning of national programmes in meteorology, 
climate and environmental science and seismology.

Determination of creamy layer among OBCs 
3153.SHRIMATI MOHSINA KIDWAI: Will the Minister SOCIAL JUSTICE 
AND EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the fields/areas in which benefits are available to the OBCs in terms of the 
orders/instructions of Central Government; 
(b) whether such benefits are not available to those falling in the "creamy layer"; 
(c) the criteria/guidelines for determining the "creamy layer"; 
(d) whether the basis of "creamy layer" vary in the States; if so, whether 
Government have information about how the States have determined the "creamy 
layer"; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SOCIAL JUSTICE 
AND EMPOWERMENT (SHRIMATI SUBBULAKSHMI JAGADEESAN): 
(a) The schemes implemented by the Ministry for the welfare of Other 
Backward Classes are:— 
(i) Pre-matric Scholarships of OBC students; 
(ii) Post-matric Scholarships for OBC Students; 
(iii) Hostels for OBC boys and girls; 
(iv) Assistance to Voluntary Organisations working for the welfare of 
OBCs; and 
(v) Concessional Financial Assistance through National Backward 
Classes Finance and Development Corporation (NBCFDC). 
Reservation and other benefits:— 
(i) 27% reservation in civil posts and services under the Government of 
India; 
(ii) Relaxed standards in respect of written examination/interview; 
(iii) Relaxation in upper age limit in direct recruitment by 3 years; and 
(iv) The number of attempts increased to 7 in respect of Civil Services 
Examination. 
(b) Yes, Sir. 
179 

RAJYA SABHA [15 May, 2006] 
(c) On the consideration of Expert Committee recommendations, Government of 
India has enhanced the income limit for determining the creamy layer amongst OBCs 
from Rs. 1.00 lakh.to Rs. 2.50 lakhs. 
(d) and (e) The basis for determining the creamy layer among the OBCs vary from State 
to State and the States formulate their own guidelines to determine the creamy layer 
among the OBCs.

Reservation in jobs in private sector 
3155. SHRI A. VIJAYARAGHAVAN: Will the Minister of SOCIAL 
JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is any proposal for job reservation in private sector; 
(b) if so, the details thereof including the steps taken to implement above 
proposal; 
(c) whether Confederation of Indian Industries has proposed a task force to 
empower disadvantaged sections of society other than mandatory quota in job 
reservation in private sector; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) the proposed year, if any, for implementation of job reservation in private 
sector? 
THE MINISTER OF SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT 
(SHRIMATI MEIRA KUMAR): (a) and (b) In pursuance of the commitment 
contained in National Common Minimum Programme (NCPM), a Group of 
Ministers (GOM) has been constituted to examine the issue of affirmative 
action, including reservation in private sector, and to initiate a dialogue with 
industry to see how best the private sector can fulfil the aspirations of youth 
belonging to Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribes. 
(c) and (d) It is learnt that Confederation of Indian Industry (Cll) has 
constituted a Task Force on affirmative action with the following terms of 
reference:— 
(i) To identify scope and opportunity for intervention by industry; 
(ii) To draw up a specific action plan to realize this opportunity; and 
181

(iii) To draw a road map and a time-frame, (e) No specific 
time-frame can be indicated at this stage.

Report of Safai Karmachari Andolan on scavengers 
3157. SHRI NANDI YELLAIAH: Will the Minister of SOCIAL JUSTICE 
AND EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a report was submitted quite recently in the Supreme Court by 
Safai Karamachari Andolan that the human scavengers strength has increased 
to 8 lakhs; 
(b) if so, the details of the Supreme Court's orders; 
(c) the details of action taken by Government in this regard; 
(d) whether a law was enacted in 1993, banning human scavenging 
throughout the country; 
(e) if so, the number of employers prosecuted, fined and convicted, State-
wise as on date for engaging human scavengers in violation of the law banning 
human scavenging; and 
(f) if not, the reasons therefor? 
185 

RAJYA SABHA [15 May, 2006] 
THE MINISTER OF SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT 
(SHRIMATI MEIRA KUMAR): (a) to (c) A petition was filed by the Safai 
Karmachari Andolan in November, 2003. The Supreme court had asked the 
Union of India and all State and UT Governments to file counter affidavit. The next 
hearing of the case is on 21.7.2006. 
(d) Sanitation being a State subject, the Employment of Manual 
Scavengers and Construction of Dry Latrines (Prohibition) Act, 1993 was 
enacted by the Parliament after the resolutions for Central legislation were 
passed by some State Legislatures. It, interalia, provides for prohibition of 
employment of manual scavengers as well as construction or continuance 
of dry latrines and for the regulation of construction and maintenance of 
water seal latrines and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. 
(e) and (f) The State of Uttar Pradesh has filed more than 12500 prosecutions 
in the judicial courts for contravention of the provisions of the Employment of 
Manual Scavengers and Construction of Dry Latrines (Prohibition) Act, 1993. 
The rest of information is being collected from the Ministry of Urban Employment 
and Poverty Alleviation, which is implementing the Act.

Identification of the forest dependent communities 
3162. SHRI V. HANUMANTHA RAO:  Will the Minister of TRIBAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have made any study to identify the forest-
dependent communities who have total dependency on the forests; 
(b) whether Government will grant any rights to such communities living in 
tribal villages and also grant them new rights under the proposed legislations; 
and 
(c) the details of steps proposed to give forest rights to forest-dependent 
people? 
THE MINISTER OF TRIBAL AFFAIRS (SHRI P. R. KYNDIAH): (a) The 
Ministry has not undertaken any study to identify the forest dependent 
communities. 
(b) and (c) The Ministry of Tribal Affairs has introduced a Scheduled 
Tribes (Recognition of Forest Rights) Bill, 2005 in the Lok Sabha on 
13.12.2005, which seeks to recoghise and vest certain rights relating to forest 
land in forest dwelling scheduled tribes, who have been residing in such forests 
for generations but whose rights have not been recorded, and to provide a 
framework for recording the forest right s so vested. The Bill when enacted 
would recognise the rights of forest dwelling scheduled tribes relating to (a) 
tenurial security; (b) livelihood, in terms of agriculture and ownership of minor 
forest produce, including rights to collect, trade and process the same; and (c) 
traditional and customary rights. The Scheduled Tribes (Recognition of Forest 
Rights) Bill, 2005 has been referred to a Joint Committee of both the Houses for 
examination.

Malnutrition in Children 
3174. SHRI SANJAY RAUT: Will the Minister of WOMEN AND CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that there is growing percentage of malnutrition 
problems among children in the country, particularly in the Maharashtra State 
for the last two years; 
205 

RAJYA SABHA [15 May, 2006] 
(b) if so, Government's response thereto; and 
(c) the details of steps taken so far by Government for tackling this issue in 
the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) According to 
studies, the underweight prevalence among children declined from 53.4% 
[National Family Health Survey-1:1992-93] to 47% [National Family Health 
Survey-2: 1998-99] in the country. In the State of Maharashtra, the prevalence 
of underweight in children declined from 54.2% to 49.6% during this period. 
(b) and (c) The problem of malnutrition is multi-dimensional and inter-
generational in nature which needs to be tackled through holistic coordinated 
interventions in areas of food security, sanitation and safe drinking water, 
nutrition, family welfare and poverty alleviation. 
To tackle the problem of malnutrition, the Government of India has 
introduced several programmes being implemented by various Ministries/ 
Departments which include: 
(i) Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) Scheme; 
(ii) National Nutritional Anaemia Control Programme, (Ministry of 
Health and Family Welfare); 
(iii) National Prophylaxis Programm e against Blindness due to Vitamin-
A, (Ministry of Health & Family Welfare); 
(iv) National Iodine Deficiency Control Programme, (Ministry of Health and 
Family Welfare); 
(v) Reproductive and Child Health Programme, (Ministry of Health and 
Family Welfare); 
(vi) Poverty Alleviation Programme, (Ministry of Rural Development); 
(vii) National Programme for Nutritional support to Primary Education 
(Mid-day Meal Scheme), (Department of Elementary Education and 
Literacy); 
(viii) Targeted Public Distribution System, (Department of Food and 
Consumer Affairs); 
206 

[15 May, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(ix) A Pilot project in 51 districts to provide free foodgrains to 
undernourished adolescent girls and pregnant and nursing mothers, 
(Planning Commission); 
(x) National Rural Health Mission (Ministry of Health and Family Welfare). 
In so far as Ministry of Women and Child Development is concerned it is 
administering ICDS Scheme which aims at holistic development of children 
below the age of 6 years and pregnant and lactating mothers. The steps taken in the 
recent past to increase the effectiveness of the delivery of services under the 
Scheme include: 
 Expansion of the Scheme from existing 5652 Projects and 7.54 lakh 
Anganwadi centres to 6118 Projects and 9.46 lakh Anganwadi Centres 
which includes 416 Projects and 78551 Anganwadi Centres in 
Maharashtra. 
 Doubling of financial norms for supplementary nutrition. 
 Sharing of 50% cost of supplementary nutrition with the States. 
 Constant emphasis on States to: 
 
 Ensure regular supply of supplementary nutrition as per schematic 
norms; 
 Ensure effective convergence of health, nutrition, education and safe 
drinking water services under various programmes.

GOVERNMENT BILLS 
The Delhi Laws (Special Provision) Bill, 2006 
THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPME NT (SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY): 
Sir, I beg to move: 
That the Bill to make special provisions for the. areas of Delhi for a period of 
one year and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto, as passed 
by Lok Sabha, be taken into consideration. 
Mr. Deputy chairman, Sir, as the hon. Members are aware, the large 
immigration of people from all over the country over the years into the National 
Capital Territory of Delhi has resulted in a huge growth in demand for residential and 
commercial space as envisaged in the master plan, 
242 

[15 May, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
1962 notified under the Delhi Development Plan 1857. The Government adopted 
planned development of Delhi through large-scale acquisition of land and 
development and disposal of such land through the Delhi Development 
Authority for meeting the needs of the people for residential, commercial and other 
spaces; However, the problems and operationalisation of the plan, poor enforcement 
and inadequacy and unaffordability of shelter, particularly for the poor have led to 
growth of slums, unauthorized construction, large-scale commercialization of 
residential areas, especially along the major roads. The Government of India has 
taken note of these deficiencies and has now places emphasis on the need for 
alternative policy options to secure proper development of Delhi. 
With this objective, the draft Master Plan for Delhi has been prepared with the 
perspective of 2021. About 7,000 suggestions and objections received from the 
public are under examination. Finalisation of the Master Plan is likely to take 
sometime. In the meantime , the Government have constituted a Committee, 
headed by Shri Tejender Khanna, former Lieutenant Governor of Delhi, to 
suggest a comprehensive strategy to deal with issues relating to unauthorized 
construction and misuse of premises. It s recommendations will be taken into 
consideration in finalizing the Plan. 
As regards the problems of those liv ing in slums and Jhuggi Jhonpris, the 
Government proposed to deal with the matter with requisite compassion, and the 
need for proper shelter and basic services for the urban poor. But, given the 
dwindling availability of land for relocation of slum dwellers, it has become imperative 
to revisit the current policy and look for more sustainable solution for their 
rehabilitation. 
There are also a large number of street vendors indifferent parts of Delhi. While 
the local bodies are formulating schemes in pursuance to the National Policy on 
street vendors; it has to be ensured that schemes are realistic and take into 
consideration not only the concerns of vendors and squatters but also citizens' 
access to public places. This is also required sometime for finalisation. 
In the meantime, a number of representations were received by the 
Government against demolition and ceiling of premises by the local bodies. Several 
hon. Members of this August House as we ll as the elected representatives of 
the Delhi have been demanding for intervention to sort out the complex issue that 
has led to the present situation. While, a large number of persons are affected by 
the on-going drives, at the same time, there is a wide divergence of public 
opinion and views to deal with this 
243 

RAJYA SABHA [15 May, 2006] 
issue. These have been taken into account while finalizing comprehensive and balance policy 
on each of these complex issues. This process would involve ground level survey, collection 
of requisite data, its analysis and consultations with the resident societies by the local 
bodies. Professional expert organization may also to be involved to formulate a 
sustainable strategy. This is a time-consuming exercise. So, Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, it 
will be noted that for the finalization of the norms, policy guidelines and feasible strategies in 
respect of problems mentioned by me earlier, a period of about one year will be required. 
While this exercise is taken up by the Government and its agencies, it is necessary and 
desirable to maintain a status quo in respect of these categories of unauthorized 
developments existing as on 1st January, 2006, so as to prevent unnecessary and 
avoidable hardship and harassment of the people. The Government, therefore, considered 
it necessary and desirable to enact the Delhi Laws (Special Provisions) Bill, 2006, for this 
purpose. 
Sir, in the facts and circumstances of the matter as mentioned by me and in order to 
meet the aforesaid objects, I move for consideration of the Delhi Laws (Special Provisions) Bill, 
2006, as passed by Lok Sabha. Thank you.

Ostensibly, the purpose of the Bill is noble. The purpose of the Bill is that there is a 
30-40 years mess which has been created and we need to sort it out; we need to 
help people out from this miserable situation; we need a little breathing time to clear 
this mess out and, therefore, till then, we willl not demolish anything or seal 
anything. But, in the process, we must do it in a manner that it is sustainable. We 
cannot do it in a manner which appears to be an eye wash. We cannot do it in a 
manner which becomes prime facie unsustainable. We pass a law and then we 
suddenly realise that the constitutionality of the law runs into serious forms of 
trouble. We may sit here and share Mr. Jai Prakash Aggarwal's anger and say we are 
angry with the court; but then they will do their job of determining the 
constitutionality. Let me say what, in effect, will be the effect of this sub-clause (2). 
Sir, the Constitution of India has divided the powers of various organs of the 
State. We, as legislatures have our own powers. Courts have their own powers. You 
have constitutional courts created by the Constitution. Those constitutional courts 
have powers under Articles 32 and 226, which are constitutional power. When 
Articles 226 and 32 were introduced in the Constituent Assembly, Dr. Ambedkar 
had said that these were the Articles which were the soul of the Constitution; 
without these, the rest of the Constitution will become meaningless because there 
will be no enforceability of the other provisions. Now, courts, in pursuance of that 
jurisdiction, have passed certain orders, or, in the course of the next one year, 
till 31st December, 2006, may pass some more orders; you have not suspended 
the municipal law; you have not sus pended the Master Plan; you have not 
suspended the sealing power. So, the courts will continue to act and pass their 
orders. Effectively, whatever orders courts now will pass under Article 32 and Article 
226, for a period of one year, will remain inoperative. Are we, therefore, trying to 
suggest that we have chosen a legal course by which the constitutional jurisdiction of 
the constitutional courts in relation to municipal matters of Delhi will remain 
suspended for a period of one year? If that is the course we have chosen, there will 
be serious question marks and doubts created whether this is the correct course 
we have followed. 
What then is the correct court? The correct course is known to any st udent 
who studies this subject. If courts have given judgments which we disagree with, 
Parliament does not have the power say, in one line, that the judgment stands 
overruled. The separation of powers.principle' does not permit that. But 
Parliament is empowered to say that the basis on which the judgement was 
given, the foundation of that judgement, was a certain law; we change that law 
and since the basis and the foundation of that judgement is gone, the judgement 
itself is gone. That is legally the

correct way of doing it. What this law does is, It does not do anything to the Master 
Plan, the sealing power, the demolition power; it allows them to exist, but merely 
says courts orders enforcing that power will not be operative for a period of one 
year. 
So, you don't change the basis on which the Supreme Court had decided, or, the High 
Court had decided, or, the High Court had decided those cases. All you are doing 
is, by a one line order you are saying, 'the constitutional jurisdiction of courts will not

method may eventually become very short-lived, and really not very sustainable.

course which can be sustained before other authorities also. Thank you, Sir.

SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY: In Delhi, we are facing an extraordinary situation. Millions of 
residents of Delhi are, rightly or wrongly, on the wrong side of law. Even as a Cabinet 
Minister, I may make bold to say that if millions of people in Delhi are on the wrong side of 
the law, there must be something wrong with the law itself. We are, therefore, facing a 
huge systemic crisis. You cannot set it right by saying that no irregularity will remain. It 
would be like Savonarola telling people of Rome 'I would rather burn down Rome than put up 
with sin'. I can't be Savonarola or Nadir Shah. Therefore, we need to realise that this is a 
problem which has developed over decades. Delhi was not built in a day; nor shall we allow 
Delhi to be demolished in a day. I agree with Mr. Arun Jaitley when he offered his 
analysis on situation in Delhi. But, I am afraid I can not share his legal pessimism. This 
Bill does take care of legal aspects adequately. I draw the attention of the House to 
Section 3 (1), "Notwithstanding anything contained in any relevant law or any rules, 
regulations or bye-laws made thereunder, the Central Government shall within a period of one 
year of the coming into effect of this Act, take all possible measures to finalise norms, policy 
guidelines and feasible strategies to deal with the problem of unauthorised development 
with regard to the under-mentioned categories" and so on and so forth. This Bill directs the 
Government of India and its agencies to perform certain tasks. The laws referred to in 
this section have been defined in the above sections. I am not getting into such detail. 
Therefore, in Section 3(2), we said 'subject to the provisions contained in sub-section 3(1)' 
and then I said notwithstanding any decree from the court. Therefore, I believe that 
legality of the Bill cannot be seriously questioned. However, this moratorium has been 
provided not only to provide relief to the affected, but to provide breathing time to the apparatus 
of the Government also. Having regard to the magnitude of the problem, we need time. This has 
been widely appreciated in this House. I am thankful to all sides of the house for this 
appreciation. 
Jai Parkash Aggarwalji was wondering as to what would happen to those who have 
filed affidavits; whether the sealed shops will be de-sealed. I believe, once this becomes law, all 
the shops will be de-sealed and those who filed affidavits will not be affected even after the 
last week of June. This is our understanding. This is the understanding given to me by our 
law officers. The Supreme Court was only dealing with one aspect of the system, namely, 
shopkeepers. That is a very important aspect. There are nearly half a million shops, big 
medium and small. But, there are also

DR. KARAN SINGH (NCT of Delhi): Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, I rise with a very heavy 
heart and express, I think, on behalf of all sections of the House our deep anguish and distress 
at the terrible events that took place recently in Doda and Udhampur. Dr. Murli Manoharji in his 
eloquent and, I must say, very balanced speech had several times referred to Jammu and 
Kashmir as my मातृभूिम Let me make one thing clear. For me, आसेतु िहमालय पयर्तम the 
whole of India is my motherland, but, certainly I have a special link with the State, Sir, 
which was built by my ancestors of very different ethnic groups brought together in one of 
the great achievements of the 19th Century, the creation of the State of Jammu and 
Kashmir in North India, a State which consolidated the northern borders of India in a fashion 
which would not have been possible had the chaos after the Sikh empires collapsed and the 
Russian advance and British imperialism. Between them, India would not have had its borders 
up where it is today. So, I am proud to belong to that State and as far as the State being a part 
of India, I can say with some pride, Sir, that the day my father signed the Instrument of 
Accession, legally and constitutionally, this whole State of Jammu and Kashmir has 
become part of India. Whether that is under our control or not, that is a different matter. I 
do not want to go into all the ramifications of the Jammu and Kashmir Policy, but it is 
correct that ever since 1947 there has been one attack after the other on behalf of 
Pakistan. The first invasion took place in 1947 itself, and, as you are aware, took place even 
before the Instrument of Accession had been signed and that war continued ultimately until the 
first of January, 1949. Then in 1965, there were the infiltrators which came in, in 
numbers.They also ended up finally in the 1965 war. Then, in 1971 there was a war. Then, 
in 1989, Sir, ever since V.P. Singh's Government came into power and there was a release 
of hostages, if you remember in the unfortunate circumstances, from that day from 1989, 
till yesterday, the 17 years have been a grim and bloody saga of ruthless killings, of 
bombings, of anti-insurgency operations necessarily by the security forces and the whole 
State has been in turmoil. Dr. Joshiji has also said that this is not an occasion for 
mutual recriminations. I have also got statistics with me as to which year what
